===== FILE 20686__1.pdf =====
VIA REGULATIONS.GOV  
 
September 3, 2025 
  
Douglas A. Collins  
Secretary of Veterans Affairs  
U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs   
810 Vermont Ave., NW  
Washington, DC 20420  
  
Re: Department of Veterans Affairs – Reproductive Health Services Proposed Rule (RIN 
2900-AS31) 
  
Dear Secretary Collins,  
  
The National Abortion Federation (NAF) hereby submits this comment on the 
Department of Veterans Affairs’ (“VA”) proposed rule entitled Reproductive Health Services 
and published in the Federal Register on August 4, 2025 (90 Fed. Reg. 36,415) (“Proposed 
Rule”). NAF opposes the rule and urges the VA to withdraw it in its entirety. 
 
NAF is the largest professional membership association for abortion providers, 
supporting our members across the United States in delivering patient-centered, evidence-based 
care. Our members include clinics specializing in abortion care (both brick-and-mortar and 
virtual clinics), health centers that provide abortion care within a broader primary care or OB-
GYN practice, hospitals, physicians and clinicians, administrators, researchers, and advocates. 
Among other activities, NAF provides educational resources for health care providers and 
publishes the authoritative medical standards for quality abortion care in the Americas: the 
Clinical Policy Guidelines for Abortion Care (“CPGs”).  
  
Current law provides very limited abortion coverage to veterans (and their family 
members under the Civilian Health and Medical Program of the Department of Veterans Affairs, 
“CHAMPVA”) for cases in which the life or health of a pregnant beneficiary is endangered or 
the pregnancy is the result of rape or incest.  The Proposed Rule would eliminate this 
coverage.  This radical contraction of coverage would have profoundly harmful effects on the 
health of America’s veterans and their family members.  Further, the Proposed Rule is contrary 
to the VA’s statutory authority, arbitrary and capricious, and otherwise not in accordance with 
law, and therefore would be unlawful if finalized.  NAF strongly urges the VA not to finalize this 
rule and to preserve critically needed abortion coverage to protect health and in cases of rape and 
incest. 
 
 
 

2 
 
The Proposed Rule Would Create Egregious Harms That the Proposed Rule Does Not 
Consider, Address, or Explain  
 
Currently, the VA offers limited coverage of abortion care in cases where the health of 
the veteran (or their CHAMPVA-enrolled family member) is endangered or where the pregnancy 
is the result of rape or incest.  38 C.F.R. §§ 17.38(c), 17.272(a)(58).  The Proposed Rule’s 
characterization of the current paradigm of limited coverage as a broader “Federal entitlement to 
abortion for veterans”1 is inaccurate and disingenuous.  The VA cannot rely on this 
mischaracterization to side-step its obligations to provide needed coverage to veterans and to 
explain why it is ending coverage for abortion care in cases where the health of the veteran is 
endangered or where the pregnancy is the result of rape or incest.  The VA does not, and cannot, 
explain this policy decision. 
 
Imposing restrictions and regulations on clinicians rather than allowing them to use their 
best clinical judgment does not allow patients to make the best decisions for their own life and 
health. NAF strongly urges the VA to retain the current coverage for abortion care when 
necessary to protect the health of a pregnant veteran (or pregnant family member) or in cases of 
rape or incest. The following are just some examples of instances in which a pregnant person’s 
health could be endangered but the situation might not rise to the level (at least immediately) of 
threatening the patient’s life: 
 
• Severe preeclampsia at 18-20 weeks gestation, where the blood pressure is dangerously 
elevated, but not yet at the threshold for eclampsia. Continuation of this pregnancy 
without termination can lead to permanent kidney damage, chronic hypertension, and 
increased long-term cardiovascular risks. See ACOG Practice Bulletin #222. 
• A patient with a history of congenital heart disease becomes pregnant and develops 
symptoms of heart failure in the second trimester. Continuing this pregnancy may worsen 
the heart problems, leading to permanent heart damage, reduced heart function, and 
lifelong physical limitations. Timely pregnancy termination is sometimes the only 
intervention to prevent irreversible heart damage. 
• A patient with lupus or instances in which the body produces abnormal antibodies 
experiences a flare mid-pregnancy. Continuing the pregnancy may result in an increased 
risk of blood clots in the arteries and veins. This can lead to complications such as deep 
vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, stroke, or heart attack. 
• A patient has ruptured membranes in the second trimester, putting the patient at risk of 
life-threatening infection. Delays in abortion care may lead to severe maternal morbidity 
and maternal death. 
• A patient is diagnosed with placenta accreta spectrum, a life-threatening condition that 
may lead to hemorrhage, hysterectomy, and maternal death. The American College of 
Obstetricians and Gynecologists and Society of Maternal Fetal Medicine recommend that 
termination of pregnancy be offered to patients with this condition due to the risk of poor 
maternal and fetal outcomes. See ACOG Obstetric Care Consensus Statement #7, Dec 
 
1 Proposed Rule, 90 Fed. Reg. at 36,416. 

3 
 
2018, https://www.acog.org/clinical/clinical-guidance/obstetric-care-
consensus/articles/2018/12/placenta-accreta-spectrum.   
 
With only the narrowest exception for abortion care when “the life of the mother would 
be endangered,” the Proposed Rule would radically constrict health care coverage, leaving 
veterans and their family members without coverage for abortions necessary to protect health or 
in cases of rape or incest.  This is particularly concerning because veterans already face increased 
health risks during pregnancy due to higher rates of chronic medical and mental health 
conditions that may increase pregnancy risks.2  Yet the Proposed Rule, in eliminating abortion 
care when necessary for veterans’ health, does not even attempt to consider or justify these 
impacts.  Reinstating the broad VA exclusion on abortion and abortion counseling poses a 
significant risk to veterans with high-risk pregnancies, chronic medical conditions, and trauma 
histories. Even when life is not immediately threatened, delayed or denied access can result in 
permanent organ damage, loss of fertility, chronic pain, psychiatric morbidity, and functional 
impairment. 
 
Further, the Proposed Rule’s wholesale exclusion of abortion care for those veterans 
whose pregnancy is a result of rape or incest is unconscionable.  The VA cannot (and makes no 
attempt to) provide any justification for this decision.  The VA’s complete silence regarding the 
need for abortion coverage in cases of rape is particularly egregious in light of the VA’s 
recognition of the pervasiveness of military sexual trauma,3 which places veterans at high risk of 
pregnancy as a result of rape.  Military sexual trauma also results in chronic health care 
challenges that can increase pregnancy risks and/or be exacerbated by pregnancy. 
 
Finally, the Proposed Rule is unworkable. Vague exemptions do not ensure access to care 
and often cause delays or denials. Even when exemptions exist, insurance or administrative staff 
frequently deny coverage, citing unclear criteria, leaving patients to appeal or pay out-of-pocket, 
causing delays in medically necessary care. Examples include: 
 
• A patient with severe hypertension in pregnancy requests a medically indicated abortion. 
The treating provider is uncertain if the patient qualifies under vague exemptions, leading 
to multiple administrative reviews. The delay results in worsening preeclampsia and 
hospitalization that could have been avoided, or permanent kidney damage, chronic 
hypertension, and increased long-term cardiovascular risks. 
• A veteran lives in a state where abortion is legally protected. The reinstatement of 
VA/CHAMPA exclusions creates conflicting policies - the state allows the procedure, but 
VA benefits do not cover it. This leads to confusion for both patients and providers 
 
2 See Joan L. Combellick et al, Severe Maternal Morbidity Among a Cohort of Post-9/11 Women Veterans, 29 J. 
Women’s Health 577 (2020) (finding severe maternal morbidity to affect a significant number of veteran women, 
and concluding the VA is uniquely positioned to develop innovative comanagement strategies). 
3 See A. Street et al., PTSD: National Center for PTSD, Dept. of Veterans 
Affairs, https://www.ptsd.va.gov/professional/treat/type/sexual_trauma_military.asp (last updated March 25, 2025) 
(“when screened, about 1 in 3 women and 1 in 50 men report having experienced [military sexual trauma] at some 
point during their military service.”); see also Service Women’s Action Network v. Sec’y of Veterans Affairs, 815 
F.3d 1369, 1372 (Fed. Cir. 2016) (noting that between 2008 and 2013 alone, veterans filed over 29,000 claims 
related to service-connected disabilities caused by military sexual trauma). 

4 
 
regarding where, how, and whether care will be covered. Providers may hesitate to 
schedule care or transfer patients due to uncertainty about coverage, liability, or 
paperwork, leading to further delays in access. 
• Due to state abortion bans or restrictions, veterans may need to travel out of state to 
obtain abortion care, but a lack of coverage creates financial and logistical barriers, 
increasing the risk of delays or unsafe procedures. 
• Patients with high-risk medical conditions (see above) require timely, coordinated care. 
Exclusions complicate the coordination, sometimes forcing clinicians to choose between 
delaying treatment or risking out-of-pocket costs for the patient.  
 
The proposed reinstatement of exclusions is highly likely to delay care, create confusion, and 
impose unnecessary administrative and financial barriers for veterans and their families. Even 
when vague exemptions exist, they often fail to ensure timely access to clinically necessary care, 
particularly for complex or high-risk pregnancies. 
 
For all of these reasons, the proposed contraction of needed coverage is unexplained, 
arbitrary, and capricious.  NAF is deeply concerned about the harmful impacts that the Proposed 
Rule would have on the health of America’s veterans and their family members, and strongly 
urges the VA not to finalize this rule or otherwise limit the VA’s and CHAMPVA’s already 
narrow and targeted abortion coverage. 
 
The Proposed Rule Does Not Comport With The Language or Intent of its Authorizing 
Statute and is Fundamentally Invalid 
 
The Proposed Rule is a fundamentally flawed departure from the VA’s current, limited 
coverage for abortion in cases where the health of the veteran is endangered or where the 
pregnancy is the result of rape or incest.  The VA is incorrect to suggest that statutory 
requirements bar it from providing abortion care.  Rather, the VA’s statutory authority compels it 
to determine coverage based on “need,” 38 U.S.C. § 1710(a), and as a result, the VA must 
evaluate when abortion coverage is needed to determine the scope of coverage.  The Proposed 
Rule does not contain this statutorily required evaluation, and because the VA cannot explain 
why current coverage to protect health and in cases of rape or incest is not needed, the proposed 
elimination of this coverage cannot be finalized. 
 
1. The Proposed Rule is entirely out of step with the statute’s history and intent, which 
evidences a clear focus on clinical necessity.  38 USC § 1710(a)(1) and (2) state that, for several 
groups of veterans, the Secretary shall furnish hospital care and medical services that the 
Secretary determines to be needed, with no exclusions for abortion.  Likewise, § 1710(a)(3) 
allows for the furnishing of necessary care to other veterans not described in (1) and 
(2).  Congress enacted this section to create a simple standard for VA eligibility based on a 
clinically appropriate need for care, “thereby ensuring that medical judgment rather than legal 
criteria will determine when care will be provided and the level at which that care will be 
furnished.”  H.R. Rep. No. 104-690, at 4 (1996) (emphasis added). 
 
 
 

5 
 
The Proposed Rule is antithetical to this legislative intent.  The proposed revision to 38 
C.F.R. § 17.272 would allow veterans and their spouses, children, survivors, and caregivers to 
receive abortion care only if a “physician certifies that the life of the mother would be 
endangered if the fetus were carried to term.”  As illustrated by the examples described above, 
this is a dangerously narrow exemption that does not allow for abortion care in a host of 
circumstances that could seriously harm a pregnant veteran (or a pregnant family member), and 
thus does not “preserve [their] health,” 38 C.F.R. § 17.38(b). 
 
The VA argues that it is authorized to enact this extreme limitation on abortion care 
because its “decision to restore VA’s medical benefits package to its pre-2022 state is consistent 
with VA’s decades-long interpretation of the law.”  We disagree. 
 
As the VA itself stated in 2024,4 the VA’s unexplained exclusion of abortion from their 
medical benefits package between 1999 and 2022 does not suggest that the VA lacked authority 
to cover this medical service.  The only time the Secretary has assessed the need for abortion 
coverage in the VA’s medical benefits package at all was in 2022 and 2024, and at both times the 
agency concluded that coverage of abortion care in limited circumstances was clinically 
necessary.  The Proposed Rule provides no reasoning to explain how circumstances have 
changed such that it is accurate or reasonable for the VA to now determine abortion care is no 
longer clinically necessary in those limited cases of rape or incest or to protect the life or health 
of the veteran (or a pregnant family member).  The Proposed Rule’s elimination of such 
coverage is a wholly unexplained reversal that ignores, without justification, the VA’s 2022 and 
2024 evidence-based determinations.5 
 
The same is true for the Proposed Rule’s treatment of abortion care under 
CHAMPVA.  The Proposed Rule asserts that “abortion is not a ‘needed’ VA service for the same 
reasons that it is not ‘medically necessary and appropriate for the treatment of a condition’ under 
CHAMPVA.”  But again, the VA does not and cannot provide any suitable explanation for its 
novel determination that abortion would not be medically necessary in any circumstance other 
than when “the life of the mother would be endangered.” 
 
In effect, the Proposed Rule’s approach allows state law to determine whether veterans 
and their family members can receive abortion care by setting coverage parameters based on the 
most restrictive state laws, Proposed Rule, 90 Fed. Reg. at 36,416.  This delegation is 
inappropriate for a federal program.  Congress instructed the VA to provide coverage to veterans 
and their family members based on clinical necessity, and the VA cannot delegate its coverage 
determination responsibility to the most restrictive state law. 
 
The VA’s Proposed Rule, if enacted, would not be supported by a reasoned explanation 
and thus would be arbitrary and capricious.  This is not an error the VA can fix through further 
elaboration: the VA’s decision is also entirely out of step with the VA’s statutory obligations and 
intentions to provide comprehensive, clinically necessary medical services.  This Proposed Rule 
cannot legally be finalized. 
 
 
4 Reproductive Health Services, 89 Fed. Reg. 15,451, 15,454 (March 4, 2024) (Final Rule). 
5 Reproductive Health Services, 87 Fed. Reg. 55,287, 55,291 (Sept. 9, 2022) (Interim Final Rule). 

6 
 
2. The Proposed Rule cannot be saved by any reliance on the VA’s authorizing statute, 
which in no way prohibits the VA from providing abortions.  In the Proposed Rule, the VA 
asserts that its “authority to provide abortions is, at least, dubious and, at most, 
nonexistent.”  This argument entirely turns on an uncodified provision of the Women Veterans 
Health Programs Act of 1992 (Pub. L. 102-585, tit. 1), which preceded Congress’s significant 
overhaul to veterans’ health care in 1996.  The VA in the Proposed Rule acknowledges that 
“[w]hile it is possible that Congress intended the 1992 restriction to continue to apply after the 
dramatic revisions of 1996, it is also possible to conclude that Congress’ intent in 1996 was to 
provide a new, full, and expansive set of laws governing authorization for VA care.”  The latter 
of these interpretations is correct and is the only interpretation that is consistent with the VA’s 
longstanding coverage of services for services that would otherwise be excluded under the 1992 
law. 
 
The 1996 Veterans’ Health Care Eligibility Reform Act effectively overtook section 106 
of the 1992 Act, allowing for general reproductive health services excluded in section 106(a)(3) 
to be provided pursuant to other sections of the Act.  In 1999, the VA implicitly construed 38 
U.S.C. § 1710 as authorizing all needed care, including services that were previously excluded 
under section 106(a)(3).  For example, since 1999, the VA has provided broad coverage for 
pregnancy and delivery services and infertility care (short of in vitro fertilization) pursuant to its 
authority in 38 USC § 1710, notwithstanding the general exclusion of such coverage under 
section 106.  The Proposed Rule rightly does not include any reduction in coverage for these 
services, further confirming that the words “under this section” in section 106 have a limiting 
meaning and section 106 does not apply to coverage under 38 U.S.C. § 1710.  As such, “section 
106’s prohibition on providing certain services ‘under this section’ simply is no longer 
operative.”6 
 
Given all of this, the best reading of the statutory framework in no way prohibits the VA 
to provide abortion care.  See Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369, 400 (2024) 
(“In the business of statutory interpretation, if it is not the best, it is not 
permissible.”).  Accordingly, and especially given the VA’s own present acknowledgement that 
it’s possible that the section 106 exclusion ceased to apply following the 1996 legislative 
revision, it is a nonsensical jump for the VA to conclude its authority to provide abortion care 
under its authorizing statute is “at least dubious.” 
 
The VA’s Proposed Rule is fundamentally out of sync with the VA’s authorizing 
statutory text and is arbitrary and capricious.  Moreover, it would pose significant harms to 
veterans and their family members.  Accordingly, NAF urges the VA to withdraw and not 
finalize the Rule.
